extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, scholarly-communication professionals, and policymakers interested in peer review and Open Science
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic review and taxonomy-building task to identify and define the distinct traits/configurations that authors and the literature use when they refer to 'open peer review' (OPR). The output is a typology intended to clarify what counts as OPR and how different traits address problems in traditional peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers are aware of each other’s identity (also called signed or unblinded review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose and theorized benefits: increases accountability, enables credit for reviewers, may expose conflicts of interest, and could motivate reviewers to invest more care. Potential downsides: may cause self-censorship and lead reviewers to temper criticism; empirical evidence is limited and mixed (studies mostly from medicine show little effect on detection of errors). Notes/examples: contrasts to single-blind and double-blind models; very prevalent in OPR definitions (present in ~90.1% of definitions reviewed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Review reports (full reports or summaries) are published alongside the relevant article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose and theorized benefits: makes otherwise hidden scholarly discussion available for reuse, increases transparency and accountability, can incentivize reviewers by making reviews part of scholarly record, helps readers evaluate editorial decisions and lingering reservations. Evidence and caveats: may increase reviewer refusal rates and time taken to write reviews (van Rooyen et al.), with no clear demonstrated improvement in review quality; some journals publish reports without reviewer names (e.g., EMBO Reports). Links to systems: ORCID and similar can be used to credit review work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider community is able to contribute to the review process (crowdsourced/public/community review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation variants: contributions may be open to anyone (anonymous or registered) or restricted to credentialed participants (e.g., ORCID with publications). Often complements invited peer review. Purpose: broaden reviewer pool, include horizontally-organized or non-traditional perspectives, counter insular/replicating reviewer pools. Risks/considerations: credentials/quality control options vary; evidence about effectiveness is limited and context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct reciprocal discussion between author(s) and reviewers, and/or between reviewers, is allowed and encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose and theorized benefits: facilitates dialogue to resolve disputes, improve manuscripts, and make the review process more collaborative and educative. Implementation: can be synchronous or asynchronous, forum-style or mediated by editors/platforms. Considerations: may blur lines between editorial selection and technical review; potential to improve clarity but may introduce social dynamics that influence candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open pre-review manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are made immediately available (e.g., via preprint servers) in advance of any formal peer review procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also described as posting preprints before formal review. Purpose: speed dissemination, invite early feedback from a wide audience, and decouple access to content from formal editorial timelines. Examples: arXiv and other preprint servers. Considerations: terminology can be ambiguous; evidence and norms vary by discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open final-version commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing or commenting on the final 'version of record' publications (post-publication comment on the final article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: enable continuing conversation and critique after formal publication; increases transparency of subsequent evaluation. Implementation: publisher comment tools, independent platforms. Usefulness: relatively uncommon among definitions (~4.9% in the reviewed corpus) but important for post-publication scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open platforms ("decoupled review")
rubrics_metrics.description: Review is facilitated by an organizational entity different from the venue of publication (peer review services decoupled from journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: separate peer review functions from publication venues to enable reuse of reviews, reduce duplicated reviewing across journals, or offer independent review services. Examples/notes: referred to as 'open platforms' or decoupled review; rare in definitions (~1.6%) but reflected in systems like PubPeer or independent review services. Considerations: raises questions about responsibilities, standards, and how review is linked to the version of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration of OPR traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Which combination of OPR traits (from the taxonomy) is present — definitions of OPR vary by configuration of traits (the paper found 22 distinct configurations of seven traits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an evaluative dimension: rather than treating OPR as monolithic, evaluate which traits are implemented together. Core/periphery: open identities and open reports form a 'core' in the literature (together cover >95% when combined with open participation for 99.2% coverage). Practical implication: comparisons or claims about 'OPR' should specify the trait configuration being discussed; many debates conflate different configurations leading to confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability and inconsistency (problem target of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review outcomes and reviewer judgments can be unreliable and inconsistent, with low inter-reviewer agreement and failures to detect methodological problems or fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a criterion to evaluate peer-review systems: does the system improve consistency and error/fraud detection? Evidence: studies show weak agreement among reviewers and inconsistent editorial outcomes; historic studies like Peters & Ceci and analyses of retractions indicate shortcomings. OPR traits claim varying capacity to address these weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and expense (problem target of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The time from submission to publication can be long and the process expensive in terms of reviewers' and editors' time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a peer-review model reduces time-to-publication and redundant reviewing across journals. OPR innovations such as preprints and decoupled platforms aim to reduce delay and duplication; however, some OPR choices (e.g., open reports) may increase reviewer time and refusal rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of accountability and risks of subversion (problem target of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional peer review's opacity can enable editors/reviewers/authors to subvert the process (e.g., bias reviewer selection, undisclosed conflicts, stolen ideas, fake reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the model increases transparency and reduces opportunities for manipulation. Open identities and open reports are theorized to increase accountability; evidence is mixed and context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and publication biases (problem target of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biases based on gender, nationality, institution, language, discipline, preference for novelty or positive results, and resistance to replications affect peer-review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative criterion: does the system mitigate or exacerbate these biases? Double-blind review aims to mitigate some biases, while open identities may reduce some unfairness but also have complex effects depending on discipline and community size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of incentives (problem target of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing is largely unpaid and anonymous, providing little recognition or reward for reviewers’ work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a model provides incentives or recognition for reviewers (e.g., through public reports, named reviews, credit via ORCID). Open reports and open identities aim to make reviewing visible for career credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wastefulness (problem target of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable reviewer comments and behind-the-scenes discussions are often hidden and not reused; useful material is wasted when reviews remain private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the model makes reviewer contributions reusable and findable (e.g., publishing reports, archiving review histories). This is an explicit rationale for open reports and some decoupled-review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of peer review: technical evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review as a mechanism to assess the validity, methodology, analysis and argumentation of scholarly work — 'is it good scholarship?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging peer-review models, assess whether they preserve or improve the rigorous technical assessment function (e.g., focus reviewers on soundness rather than novelty). Some OPR models separate technical soundness review from editorial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of peer review: editorial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review's role in guiding editorial selection decisions regarding novelty, importance, and fit for a venue — 'is it exciting, innovative or right for this journal?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models differ in how much peer review contributes to selection versus solely technical validation (e.g., PLOS ONE-style soundness-only review). Evaluate whether OPR traits clarify or confuse this selection function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'signed review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signed review — reviewers sign their reports (overlaps with open identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed in Emily Ford's schema; the paper critiques attempts that reduce multiple traits to open identities alone. Note: Ford used this as one of eight 'common characteristics' but argued that open identities might be treated as the defining element — a point the author disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'disclosed review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosed review — review reports are disclosed/published (overlaps with open reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of Ford's earlier schema; Ross-Hellauer discusses this but cautions against conflating traits or over-reducing OPR to a single feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'editor-mediated review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review processes that are mediated by editors (a characteristic Ford listed, though commonly present in traditional peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ross-Hellauer criticizes listing editor-mediated review as distinguishing OPR because it is common to traditional review; use cautiously as a differentiator for OPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'transparent review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent review — processes and decisions are made visible (a composite characteristic that may include open identities and open reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ross-Hellauer notes that 'transparent review' can be a complex of other traits (e.g., open reports + open identities) rather than a base element by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'crowdsourced review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourced review — opening reviews to a wider community (overlaps with open participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent or closely related to open participation; consider implementation details such as credential requirements and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'prepublication review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepublication review — review occurring prior to formal publication (overlaps with pre-review manuscripts / preprints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ross-Hellauer argues careful terminology is needed; 'prepublication' may be common to traditional and OPR models and can mean different things in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'synchronous review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Synchronous review — simultaneous, time-bound review interactions (a theoretical element listed by Ford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by Ford but considered a questionable or niche element; Ross-Hellauer treats some of Ford's characteristics as less central or not universally meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ford's 'post-publication review' (from prior schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication review — review or commenting after formal publication (overlaps with open final-version commenting / PPPR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to open final-version commenting; Ross-Hellauer's taxonomy treats post-publication engagement as one of several traits that can be part of OPR configurations.
